                                             PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                 §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION

                                                                      OF TEXAS
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                          §

                                                         §

CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC’S COMMENTS ON COMMISSION
      STAFF’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.194


       Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, including its wholly-owned subsidiaries under
Calpine, LLC (together, “Constellation”) welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback in
response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Staff’s Proposal for
Publication of new 16 TAC § 25.194 establishing Large Load Interconnection Standards pursuant
to the requirements of Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”) 1.
       Constellation can offer a unique perspective based on its generation assets, wholesale
businesses, and retail offerings in Texas and beyond, including participation in competitive energy
markets across the country. Our generation fleet of nuclear, hydro, wind, solar and natural gas
facilities has the generating capacity to power approximately 15 million homes, providing 10
percent of all carbon-free energy on the grid in the U.S. Additionally, Calpine LLC is America’s
largest generator of electricity from natural gas and geothermal resources with operations in
competitive power markets. The fleet of 79 energy facilities in operation represents over 27,000
megawatts of generation capacity. Through wholesale power operations in 22 states and Canada
and through retail businesses, it serves customers in 48 states and Canada, including Texas. We
are a leading competitive energy company providing power, natural gas and clean carbon-free
energy solutions to homes and businesses across the country. From electricity and natural gas
procurement to energy management options and renewable supply we empower millions of
customers – including three-fourths of the Fortune 100 – to make highly informed and strategic
energy choices.
       Constellation respectfully submits the following comments.


       1
           Senate Bill 6, 89th Leg, R.S. (2025).

                                                     1
                                              I.       INTRODUCTION

         Pursuant to the requirements of SB 6, Constellation supports adoption of a rule that
establishes transparent and uniform Large Load interconnection standards which are designed to
support business development in Texas while also minimizing the potential for stranded
infrastructure costs and which maintain the reliability of the ERCOT system. 2 To this end,
Constellation encourages the Commission to be mindful of the charge in SB 6 to balance Large
Load business development with cost and reliability concerns; as such, new 16 TAC § 25.194 must
not place so much financial burden on new Large Load customers that it becomes commercially
unviable to pursue business opportunities in Texas.

                    II.     COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

         Constellation proposes the following revisions to the below-referenced subsections of
proposed 16 TAC § 25.194:
    (b) Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks has initiated a large
         load interconnection request after the effective date of this rule for:
               (1) a new interconnection at a single site that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts
                    (MWs);
               (2) an expanded interconnection at a single site that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the
                    first time; and
               (3) an expanded interconnection at a single site that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or
                    more.

         Subsection (b) should clearly establish which large load interconnection requests
(“LLIRs”) are subject to this new rule consistent with the plain language of SB 6 and Article I,
Section 16 of the Texas Constitution, prohibiting the enactment of retroactive laws. 3 In the first
instance, PURA § 37.0561(c) indicates that the standards established by the Commission for
interconnecting large load customers “must only apply to customers requesting a new or expanded
interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed a demand threshold established


         2
             Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.0561(b).
         3
           “No bill of attainder, ex post facto law, retroactive law, or any law impairing the obligation of contracts,
shall be made”.

                                                          2
 by the commission […]” (emphasis added). The statute does not define “new or expanded
interconnection”. As Texas courts have clearly established, legislative intent should be determined
from the plain text of a statute, taking statutes as they are found, presuming the Legislature
included words that it intended to include and omitted words it intended to omit. 4 As such, for the
standards to apply to “new or expanded” large load interconnection requests, a plain reading of
this application should mean a large load interconnection request that is “new” or an “expansion”
as of the date the Commission’s adopted standards are effective. If the Legislature had intended
for the Commission’s large load interconnection standards developed under SB 6 to apply
retroactively to large load interconnection requests that were made before the rules were effective,
the Legislature could have done so, but did not.
        Secondly, if the rule were to be applicable to all pending LLIRs which have not energized
or reached their peak requested demand as of the effective date of this rule, such application would
impose retroactive rulemaking on large load applicants which have been operating under the
existing ERCOT Protocols and Planning Guide requirements for large load interconnection,
including rules which pre-date SB 6. This results in retroactive application of legislation in
violation of Texas legal precedent. For example, the Texas Supreme Court has previously held that
the Texas constitutional prohibition (cited above) against retroactive legislation would prohibit a
change in a utility’s rates that “would retroact so as to change the substantial rights and obligations
of the implied contract that exists between a utility and its customers.” 5 The Texas Supreme Court
has further held that “[l]aws may not operate retroactively to deprive or impair vested substantive
rights acquired under existing laws” but that “changes in statutes affecting remedies or procedure
may be applied retroactively.” 6 The effect of imposing new large load interconnection standards
on existing interconnection requests that pre-date SB 6 and the Commission’s implementing rule
is the deprivation or impairment of substantive rights and obligations of those large load
customers; retroactive application of the rules is not just merely a change in procedure –
particularly given the new requirements regarding financial security.


        4
           Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex. v.. Luminant Energy Co., LLC, 691 S.W. 3d 448, 461 (Jun. 14, 2024) (No. 23 -
0231) citing Tex. State Bd. of Marriage & Fam. Therapists v. Tex. Med. Ass’n, 511 S.W.3d 28, 33 (Tex. 2017) and
Union Carbide Corp. v. Synatzske, 438 S.W. 3d 39, 52 (Tex. 2014)
        5
            Southwestern Bell Telephone Company v. Pub. Util. Comm’n of Tex, et al., 615 S.W.2d 947 (Tex 1981).
        6
          Holder v. Wood, 714 S.W.2d 318, 319 (Tex. 1986); Ex Parte Abell, 613 S.W.2d 255, 260 (Tex.1981) and
Bardwell v. Anderson, 325 S.W.2d 929, 939 (Tex.Civ.App.—Houston 1959, writ ref'd n.r.e.).

                                                        3
         To further illustrate the impairment referenced above, existing large load applicants as of
the effective date of the proposed rule will have already invested significant financial capital into
developing their projects in good faith reliance on the existing rules in place prior to SB 6. Many
of them have also entered into commercial agreements with large load customer “tenants” which
have binding terms that were developed in good faith reliance on the LLIR’s ability to construct,
energize, and ramp up the requested load amount consistent with pre-SB 6 ERCOT requirements.
The Commission should not impose new rules, for the first time, on LLIRs which have advanced
through the current large load interconnection process. Doing so would be inconsistent with the
legislative directive 7 to adopt rules which support business development of large loads as these
new rules (if retroactively applied) could result in severe adverse commercial consequences for
existing LLIRs that were not previously subject to the specific financial security and
interconnection process requirements of the proposed rule. Constellation also proposes clarifying
language that each subsection of applicability relates to large load interconnection requests at a
single site to avoid any misinterpretation that a single large load customer entity that seeks various
interconnection requests at separate sites (for distinct loads) totaling 75 MW or more could be
subject to these requirements.


    (c) Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the following
    meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:


        (2)      Competitively sensitive information – Competitively sensitive information
                 includes, but is not limited to, exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or
                 property boundaries; commercial terms, such as pricing or internal development
                 prioritization; proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment
                 strategies; and financing structures; and load ramp information (if designated as
                 confidential by the interconnecting large load entity). Competitively sensitive
                 information does not include the identity of a large load customer; general site
                 location, such as load zone; requested or contracted peak demand; timing of initial



        7
          PURA § 37.0561(b) (“The commission by rule shall establish standards for interconnecting large load
customers in the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to support business development in the state while
minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability” (emphasis added)).

                                                       4
                energization; or whether an interconnection request is associated with the same
               applicant or affiliated entities. For large load customers impacted by the
               requirements of PURA Section 39.169, the following information is not considered
               competitively sensitive if so determined by the Commission: requested or
               contracted peak demand or load ramp.


       PURA § 37.0561 does not require that any specific information submitted to the relevant
interconnecting electric utility or municipally owned utility (“MOU”) be deemed not confidential
or not “competitively sensitive”. Rather, the statute errs on the side of preserving confidentiality
for competitively sensitive information which is not specifically enumerated. For example, while
PURA § 37.0561(k) indicates that the Commission’s large load interconnection standards must
establish a procedure to allow ERCOT to access any information collected by the interconnecting
utility or MOU to ensure compliance with the standards for transmission planning analysis, any
such information which is customer-specific or competitively sensitive is confidential and not
subject to disclosure under Government Code Chapter 552. PURA § 37.0561(d) additionally
indicates that while the large load interconnection standards must require a large load customer to
disclose to the interconnecting utility or MOU whether the customer is pursuing a substantially
similar request for electric service in the state which would result in the customer materially
changing, delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request, the disclosure may withhold or
anonymize competitively sensitive details.
       The draft definition for “competitively sensitive” risks being under-inclusive by providing
too limited a list of factors. The competitive nature of commercially sensitive information varies
by company and by circumstance, depending on the specifics of a given commercial transaction
and the parties thereto. Additionally, the excluded list of items from the definition conflates the
provisions of PURA Sections 37.0561 and 39.169. Through its rulemaking to implement PURA
Section 39.169 (net metering approval for co-located existing stand-alone generation resources
and new large loads), the Commission has determined that the customer’s requested peak demand
and load ramp may not be protected information for purposes of evaluating a request for approval
of a net metering arrangement between an existing stand-alone generation resource and a new co-




                                                 5
 located large load. 8 However, this policy should not categorically apply to all large load customers,
including those which will not be subject to Commission scrutiny in a net metering application
under PURA Section 39.169.
        Constellation also notes that excluding peak demand and load ramp information from the
definition of “commercially sensitive” also risks an inconsistent policy directive with ERCOT
Nodal Protocols (“ERCOT Protocols”) Section 1.3.1.1(x), which describes the following as
“Protected Information”: “Information provided by Entities under Section 10.3.2.4, Reporting of
Net Generation Capacity”. Relatedly, while the date of initial grid synchronization/energization of
a large load may not be commercially sensitive in all instances, the load ramp schedule for the
large load customer is generally considered to be highly commercially sensitive as this is not
publicly disclosed by large load developers due to competitive concerns – speed to market is a key
factor guiding business decisions in the collocation context. Additionally, a large load ramp
schedule may be commercially sensitive pursuant to the underlying agreements between the entity
that submitted an LLIR and the end-use large load customer “tenant”.


        (3)     Contracted peak demand – the total non-coincident peak demand that a large load
                customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP serve at
                a site as stated in an interconnection agreement and/or equivalent service extension
                or other agreement. Any demand at the site for which a large load customer does
                not request to be served by an interconnecting DSP or TSP shall not be included in
                the definition of “contracted peak demand”.

        In some instances, a large load customer may not request for its full demand to be served
by an interconnecting TSP or DSP. For example, consider a scenario in which a single large load
customer plans to develop consuming facilities that will require a total of 200 MW. Of the 200
MW, 100 MW will be interconnected to the ERCOT grid, either as a stand-alone, front-of-meter
large load interconnection request or as a co-located large load interconnection request sharing
interconnection facilities to the ERCOT grid with generation resource. The remaining 100 MW
will be developed and owned by the same large load customer but will not be electrically


        8
         See Rulemaking for Net Metering Arrangements Involving a Large Load Co-Located with an Existing
Generation Resource, PUCT Project No. 58479, Order Adopting New 16 TAC § 25.205 (Mar. 26, 2026); 16 TAC §
25.205 (k)(2)(D).

                                                   6
 interconnected to the facilities consuming up to 100 MW through grid-connected facilities.
Because the second 100 MW will be electrically segregated from the former, those facilities may
be served by onsite generation and will never take power from the grid. As such, the segregated
load (although owned and developed by the same large load customer as the grid-interconnected
load) should not be included in the “contracted peak demand” for the large load customer request
subject to this rule. Additionally, if the load is not co-located with a generation resource, the
applicable agreement with the interconnecting utility may not be an “interconnection agreement”
and may be an alternative form of agreement such as a Facilities Extension Agreement. ERCOT’s
currently pending Planning Guide Revision Request 145 (Batch Zero Process for Large Load
Interconnections) currently uses the phrase “interconnection agreements and/or equivalent service
extension or other agreements” in describing the sorts of agreements that must be executed with
an interconnecting TSP or DSP under the legacy standards for large load interconnection. Unless
and until a standardized “interconnection agreement” is established for large load interconnections,
this broader language should be memorialized in the rule. If a large load “interconnection
agreement” is eventually established, the rule can be revised in the future.


       (4)     Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) – The electric utility,
               municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates the
               facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system,
               which may not be the same entity as the applicable DSP and may not be the TSP
               providing generation and/or transmission service to the applicable DSP.


Constellation proposes clarifying language to address the following scenarios:


    (a) A large load customer may co-locate with a generation resource and interconnect via
        private facilities to a generator’s substation behind the existing generation point of
        interconnection (“POI”). Because the large load customer will receive grid power back-
        fed through the interconnection facilities from the TSP that interconnects the generator to
        the ERCOT grid, the large load’s consuming facilities may be physically located in the
        retail distribution service area of a DSP that is not associated with the generator’s
        interconnecting TSP. For example, a large load may co-locate with a generation resource

                                                 7
          interconnected to Oncor (the interconnecting TSP) but may physically sit within the retail
         service area of a distribution cooperative that is a member of a generation and/or
         transmission (“G/T”) cooperative. In this scenario, the G/T cooperative is not the
         interconnecting TSP. If the large load consuming facilities were physically located within
         the retail distribution service area of Oncor, then Oncor would be the TSP and the DSP.


     (b) A large load customer’s consuming facilities may be physically located within a dual-
         certificated retail delivery service area or may straddle the retail delivery service areas of
         two DSPs. In such scenarios, the customer may choose the applicable DSP. 9 It is possible
         that the interconnecting TSP will not be the same entity as the DSP in this scenario, and/or
         that the interconnecting TSP will not be the TSP which provides G/T service to the chosen
         DSP.


        (7)      Interconnection study – The set of studies that are required by ERCOT pursuant
                 to the ERCOT Protocols and Other Binding Documents before a large load
                 customer may be interconnected.


        The rule should clarify that the relevant interconnection studies are those which have been
subject to the ERCOT stakeholder process for revision requests and which have been approved by
the ERCOT Board of Directors and by the Commission. Should ERCOT determine that changes
are required to those established processes, the rule should recognize that ERCOT has an
established method for changing its processes and ensure that large load customers are not subject
to new or different requirements until the relevant ERCOT Protocols or other codified standards
have been considered and approved by all relevant entities, including the Commission, through
the established process. This will provide regulatory certainty to large load customers and their
financial partners.




        9
           See, e.g. Joint Petition for Declaratory Order of Oncor Electric Delivery Company, LLC and United
Electric Cooperative Services Regarding Service to Burleson Independent School District High School No. 2, Docket
No. 36649 (Apr. 21, 2009) and Petition of Murphy Oil Corporation for Declaratory Order Regarding Service to the
Murphy Oil Eagle Ford Leasehold Area, Docket No. 46734, Order at 3 (Oct. 25, 2018).

                                                       8
        (9)     Large load customer – An entity The Interconnecting Large Load Entity (“ILLE”)
               requesting new or expanded interconnection where the customer’s total expected
               non-coincident peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75 MW. ILLE
               shall have the meaning given in the ERCOT Protocols and Other Binding
               Documents.


       Constellation proposes revisions to this term to clarify that the “large load customer” for
purposes of compliance with the large load interconnection standards established in this rule need
not be the same entity which ultimately consumes end-use power as the retail customer. The
ERCOT Planning Guide has an existing defined term for “interconnecting large load entity”
(“ILLE”) which is the entity that submits the LLIR for purposes of developing and interconnecting
a large load project. This is the entity which should be subject to these standards – not an end-use
retail customer which is usually not involved in the large load interconnection process and
frequently does not have any ownership in the large load consuming facilities.


   (d) Intermediate agreement. Before a large load interconnection request is submitted to
       ERCOT for study, the large load customer must execute an intermediate agreement with
       the interconnecting DSP and, if different from the interconnecting DSP, the interconnecting
       TSP. If the interconnecting DSP and the interconnecting TSP are different entities, the
       intermediate agreement must specifically identify each entity’s responsibilities under this
       section, including which entity will accept the study fee and financial security from the
       large load customer. The intermediate agreement must meet the requirements of this
       subsection. Notwithstanding any other provisions of this section, if a change in fact requires
       modification to the underlying site control documentation, a large load customer is
       permitted to provide updated documentation to the interconnecting DSP or TSP and such
       update will not delay or adversely impact the large load interconnection request.
       (1)     Site control. A large load customer must demonstrate site control for the proposed
               load through provision of one or more of the following property interests to the
               interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP. Each form of documentation
               listed herein will be deemed to satisfy requirements of this section if the large load
               customer provides written confirmation to the TSP addressing each relevant issue:

                                                 9
                (A)      a signed and executed lease agreement for one or more parcels of land
                        sufficient to accommodate the customer’s planned facilities at the proposed
                        load location for a duration of at least five years from the date the large
                        load customer is expected to reach the planned contracted peak demand;
               (B)      a deed for one or more parcels of land sufficient to accommodate the
                        customer’s planned facilities at the proposed location;
               (C)      a signed and executed agreement with an option to purchase or lease one
                        or more parcels of land sufficient to accommodate the customer’s planned
                        facilities at the proposed location.

     The site control requirements for the intermediate agreement phase of an LLIR should
account for the commercial realities of large load project development. In most instances when an
ILLE is first submitting an LLIR and engaging with the interconnecting TSP and DSP to initiate
studies, the ILLE will not have a contracted end-use retail customer (often a “tenant”) to physically
use the large load’s consuming facilities. Depending on the characteristics of the specific tenant,
the acreage requirement for the same amount of MW may vary. For example, a data center tenant
may require more or less land to house the operations necessary for 200 MW of artificial
intelligence (“AI”) computing than a bitcoin mining operation would require to house the
operations necessary for 200 MW of its unique utilization. Because an ILLE may be actively
soliciting end-user tenants at the intermediate agreement phase of the large load interconnection
process, the rule should include flexibility for the large load customer to modify its site control
documentation if needed to accommodate the end-use tenant that it ultimately secures to make the
large load project commercially viable.
       As drafted, the rule does not specify how a large load customer may establish that the site
control it has secured will accommodate the customer’s planned facilities at the location, or for
how long. This could result in different TSPs establishing varying standards as to how large load
customers can satisfy the requirement. To standardize this process, the Commission should allow
the large load customer to provide the required site control components of the rule and to confirm
in writing that the requirements of each form of documentation have been satisfied.




                                                 10
        Finally, the site control requirements at the intermediate agreement phase should reference
“planned” peak demand rather than “contracted” peak demand, since there is generally no contract
yet in place with the interconnecting TSP or DSP, as applicable, to serve the load.


       (2)     Substantially similar interconnection request. A large load customer must
               disclose to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP whether the
               customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request for electric
               service, the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing,
               delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request. “Substantially similar” shall
               mean a large load interconnection request for the same amount of planned peak
               demand, having the same load and ramp characteristics as an existing
               interconnection request, intended for the same end-use customer. A material change
               or delay includes a delay of one or more years to the project’s projected date to
               realize its requested or contracted peak demand, a 20% or greater change in the
               requested or contracted peak demand, or a change in the location for the point of
               interconnection.
               (A)     A large load customer that is pursuing a substantially similar
                       interconnection request for electric service the approval of which would
                       result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the
                       interconnection request must disclose the following information to the
                       interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP, as applicable:
                       (i) – (v).
               (B)     A large load customer that discloses a substantially similar interconnection
                       request under this subsection may anonymize competitively sensitive
                       information in its disclosure to the interconnecting DSP or the
                       interconnecting TSP, as applicable.
               (C)     An interconnecting DSP and an interconnecting TSP must not sell, share,
                       or disclose information submitted to the interconnecting DSP or the
                       interconnecting TSP under this subsection other than a disclosure to the
                       commission or ERCOT, subject to appropriate confidentiality protections.



                                                11
                (D)      ERCOT may request and the large load customer must provide any
                        competitively sensitive information ERCOT deems necessary to complete
                        any analysis required as part of the interconnection process. ERCOT must
                        treat disclosed competitively sensitive information as Protected
                        Information under ERCOT protocols.
       Although SB 6 indicates that the large load interconnection standards must require each
large load customer to disclose to the interconnecting utility whether the customer is pursuing a
substantially similar request for service, the approval of which would result in a material change
to, delay to, or withdrawal of the request, it does not define “substantially similar”. This poses a
risk that various interconnecting utilities could develop differing standards as to what constitutes
a “substantially similar” request and could also cause confusion among large load developers as
to which requests they must disclose. Additionally, the recent data center boom within ERCOT
has resulted in hyperscaler tenants seeking opportunities to inhabit multiple large load facilities
that are substantially similar in demand, scale, and use but which are discrete facilities. An ILLE
in active discussions with a potential tenant may not always know if similar large load
interconnection requests meet the “change, delay, or withdrawal” standard of SB6 because that
determination may be out of their control. They therefore require a clear and easily applicable
standard for “substantially similar”.
       Constellation also proposes minor changes to clarify that such disclosure must be made to
the relevant TSP or DSP as applicable. This is to avoid any inference that the receiving entity is
discretionary. Constellation proposes that this change be made throughout the entirety of the rule.
       The Commission should include “subject to appropriate confidentiality protections” in sub-
provision (C) to align with the language of SB 6 in PURA Section 37.0561(d). The Commission
should omit sub-provision (D) in its entirety because it is not contemplated in PURA 37.0561 that
ERCOT should have such broad discretion to solicit confidential information from large load
customers. The draft rule should mirror SB 6 on such concepts as described in PURA Sections
37.0561(d) and (k). Subsection (k) gives ERCOT broad discretion to access any information
collected by the interconnecting electric utility or MOU to ensure compliance with the standards
for transmission planning analysis and that any customer-specific or competitively sensitive
information obtained under this subsection is confidential and not subject to disclosure under



                                                12
 Chapter 552, Government Code. Proposed (D) is overly broad in interpreting this statutory
language.
       (3)     Site-related studies and engineering services. A large load customer must submit
               to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP, as applicable, the large load
               customer’s plans, expected timing, and progress for site-related studies and
               engineering services required for project development before energization (e.g.,
               geotechnical survey, water, wastewater, or gas).        The submission must be
               accompanied by an attestation by an officer or official with binding authority over
               the large load customer stating that the information contained in the submission is
               complete and accurate at the time the attestation is signed. A large load customer
               must provide updates or progress reports to the applicable interconnecting DSP or
               the interconnecting TSP when requested, but no more frequently than quarterly. All
               information subject to this subsection shall be considered Protected Information
               under the ERCOT Protocols and any competitively-sensitive information shall not
               be subject to disclosure under Chapter 552, Government Code.


       The Commission should include more guidance in the rule regarding the specific
information required for the referenced submission and in quarterly update or progress reports;
this would provide regulatory certainty to large load customers. Additionally, the rule should
specify that any protected information included in these required submissions is subject to the
Protected Information provisions of the ERCOT Protocols and is not otherwise subject to
disclosure if such information is competitively sensitive.


       (4)     State and local regulatory approvals. A large load customer must submit to the
               interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP, as applicable, the large load
               customer’s plans, expected timing, and current progress for obtaining non-
               ministerial discretionary approvals from state and local regulatory authorities
               required for development before energization (e.g., water, air, or backup generation
               permits). The submission must be accompanied by an attestation by an officer or
               official with binding authority over the large load customer attesting that the
               information contained in the submission is complete and accurate at the time the

                                                13
                attestation is signed. A large load customer must provide updates or progress
               reports to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP when requested, but
               no more frequently than quarterly. All information subject to this subsection shall
               be considered Protected Information under the ERCOT Protocols and any
               competitively-sensitive information shall not be subject to disclosure under Chapter
               552, Government Code.


       Constellation proposes revisions to this subsection for the same reasons described above
regarding subsection (3).
       (6)     Backup generating facilities.         A large load customer must disclose to the
               interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP whether the customer plans to have
               on-site backup generating facilities. If the large load customer plans to have on-
               site backup generating facilities, the large load customer must also disclose the
               following information, which may be revised as updated information becomes
               available:
               (A)      an estimate of the total nameplate capacity number of backup generating
               units;
               (B)      the nameplate capacity of each of the backup generating facilities;
               (C)      the expected fuel source and operational characteristics of each of the
                        backup generating facilities, including any run hour limitations and any fuel
                        storage limitations under the existing anticipated environmental permits;
                        and
               (D)      if known, how quickly each of the backup generating facilities can reach
                        their full capacity to serve the load.


       As previously stated, at the intermediate agreement phase of large load interconnection,
the exact details related to the end-use customer characteristics may not yet be known. Similarly,
the end-use customer’s preferred backup generation capacity is often not yet known at this phase.
While the ILLE may propose as part of its commercial offering to an end-use load customer tenant
that the configuration include a certain amount of onsite backup generation, this could change
pending commercial discussions. Accordingly, Constellation proposes that the large load customer

                                                  14
 be required to disclose an estimate of the expected backup generation capacity to allow for the
possibility of revision later. Additionally, the number of backup units are not necessarily relevant
for planning purposes; the total MW capacity of the backup generation is relevant. Given that firm
plans for backup generation capacity may not yet be known at this phase of interconnection, the
rule should additionally be revised to indicate that certain of the requested information should be
provided “as expected”, “if known” or “if available” since items like environmental permits will
not have been obtained if the backup generation capacity is still subject to change. Constellation
further proposes additional language in subsection (6) allowing for the opportunity to supplement
or revise the provided information as updates become available.


       (7)     Power supply. A large load customer must disclose whether how it plans to
               consume procure power that is exclusively sourced from the ERCOT grid, or
               whether it plans to consume power that is produced by a co-located generation
               resource, and whether the large load customer will have has on-site, non-grid
               interconnected generation that will provide power exclusively to the large load
               customer and to no other loads.


       The Commission should make the above proposed changes to the rule to clarify what
specific information is being requested regarding the large load customer’s consuming facilities’
power consumption. “Procurement” seems to relate to commercial agreements which are not
necessarily relevant to utility interconnection and ERCOT planning standards. However, it may
be relevant for a large load customer to disclose how much of its demand will be served from the
